utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it was on that day because we took a walk together in Plitvice, which is a natural resort, through a wood, they have a lot of lakes there, and talked one on one on the issues which we had between us. And it was at that opportunity that I asked Mr. Hadzic to have a look at a list of names drawn by a group called Widows of Vukovar. I don't know whether this was one sheets or two sheets and I don't know how many names there were, maybe between 50 and 150, all Croatian men, and the widows or a Croatian official, I don't recall who gave that to me, asked me whether I could find out something about these people, whether they were alive or what was with them. And Hadzic then declared himself ready to have a look at this list. And I gave it to him. And he looked quietly at it and he looked attentively at it, and then he said, They are all dead. He gave the list back to me. I gave the list to the Croats. I have not kept a copy, unfortunately. That's all. We did not discuss who had killed them, for what reason they were dead or so. He just said that this was the state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was anyone else present --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- or was the just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What language was the conversation in?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: It was Serbian. I found that it was sometimes possible to talk to Hadzic one on one on issues that he would not have discussed with his people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Such as -- well, looking at the list, is that something that --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: The list, for example, yes. Then asking me for a copy of the Croatian law. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender 65 ter 5416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we move -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P2887. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While we've still got that document on the screen, if we could look at the bottom of it, paragraph 6. There's a reference to a Mr. Bjegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: He was the prime minister of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For which entity?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: The RSK. They had quite a change of prime ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. President, is tab 29. 65 ter 1801.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, again, we see this document, first of all - if we could move up a little bit - just to confirm the letterhead here. It's coming from -- where is this coming from?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Jeannie Peterson. That's the Knin -- well, now she is in Belgrade, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: But she was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you look at the top right-hand corner we see the Cyrillic text --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: That's the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then turning the page, this appears to be directed to yourself and Mr. Vollebaek?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 27th of September, 1993. Do you remember this letter?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Can you make it a bit bigger?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now you referred to already and -- Erdut, an Erdut agreement and if can you just briefly tell us what the Erdut agreement -- I think you called it Erdut 1?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Yeah, because later was on Sector East in 1995 or 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You might need to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Sorry. So there was an Erdut 2 which resolved the Sector East question after the Croats had taken the rest of the RSK. The Erdut 1 Agreement was a very short agreement, where the Croats played a very bad trick because Tudjman never had the intention to fulfil it. It was just meant to secure the solemn opening of the Maslenica bridge on the 18th of July, and later Tudjman told Vollebaek and me while he visited in Brioni that this was this letter for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the Erdut agreement that you described now, was this related to the whole issue of Maslenica and resolution --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Right, right, right. It was -- it was -- this 802 thing petered out and out, but it was one of the consequences and because of this opening of the bridge on the 18th of July, we were under pressure. It was mainly negotiated by Vollebaek because I was busy in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And looking at the bottom of this page and then we'll continue on to the next, the last paragraph here, the reference to Second World War as well as the latest confrontation. And then continuing on, over to the next page. In fact, if we could move to the bottom, you can see who the author of this is, Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: That's Bjegovic. Prime minister. It says prime minister of the republic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. The question here is, if we could move up because we're just got another minute remaining for today, he says: "There is no other solution but for the Serbian and Croatian national groups to maintain their presence in individual states. It is this factor which is foreseen by the Vance Plan, which is explicit in its interpretation that a political solution will be reached by negotiations between the two communities." The question here, Ambassador, is whether this interpretation of the Vance Plan is consistent with your own interpretation of the --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: No, it's totally wrong because the Vance Plan was to regulate a provisional state of affairs until the conference found a solution. It was up to the conference to negotiate the solution, and the separation of Serbs and Croats, this was the line of the day. Tudjman thought along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender that one, 65 ter 1801.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P2887. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Stringer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Oh, it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- you have to get back in the routine again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've been away. It's going to be good timing, then, because I should be able to finish my direct before 2.00. Could we please have tab 56. 65 ter 5478.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, we've just been looking at this document, which is from the letter from Mr. Bjegovic dated the 27th of September --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Is that the one I have here? Because that's another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Here's the new one. The question here is whether negotiations involving yourself, Mr. Hadzic, his people, as well as the Croatians, whether those continued then into November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there was this German/French initiative which more or less doubled only what the conference had proposed on the base of a cease-fire come to practical arrangements. But later in 1993 we had this meeting in Norway, a place called Voganess [phoen] where there was a serious attempt to try to solve the problems, cease-fire and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference here to day 3 final meeting attended and this is the 4th of November --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: That is -- that is the Norwegian thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if we could move -- well, first question is: Were you present and involved in these negotiations --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving to the next page of the document. Again, because the details of the negotiations are less significant. The various sides are making their closing remarks. And in paragraph 4, there's a reference to a Mr. Sarinic who --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: His name is Sarinic. He was the main Croatian negotiator for two years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And now here he's saying that the very fact that the chair in front of him was empty, the head of Serb delegations showed the attitude of the Serb delegation to signing the agreement. And then moving down the same paragraph, he says that one of the rules had been secrecy. And he indicates on the next line that if he'd been correctly informed, the head of the Serb delegation was giving a television interview. Can you comment on those remarks? What's that about?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: I mean, it had been agreed that the talks in Norway should be secret. And it seems that Mr. Hadzic has leaked these talks to Serb media. I cannot tell you how and when and whether it is hundred per cent true but it was taken for granted. I think it was not even disputed because the Serbs complained of a certain public statement by President Tudjman which contained things unacceptable to them. This remark by Mr. Sarinic refers to the fact that in the last session the chair of the head of the Serb delegation was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Whose chair was that?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic's chair. And -- well, I don't know. Mr. Hadzic sometimes had also a cavalier attitude to these things and he might have gone shopping in Norway. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The impact of the breach of secrecy, how did that affect the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Well, the Croats took it very badly and so the negotiations capsized. I don't know whether we might have come to an agreement. After this, there was one more meeting of these delegations in Serbia, in Dobanovci, which a sort of resort which, I think, Tito had developed for himself and which was one of Milosevic's residences or so. But that led nowhere, and in the end there was only an agreement of both sides not to shoot. And Vollebaek and I wrote a letter to both sides saying that we regretted that we didn't go farther and that they should indeed refrain from shooting, and then Vollebaek left the conference and Kai Eide came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender 65 ter 5478.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2889.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And if I may make a correction, 65 ter document 1801 should be assigned Exhibit Number P2888 as opposed to 2887 as it was previously assigned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ambassador Ahrens, that brings us to the end of 1993. You've already indicated your awareness that, by early 1994, Mr. Hadzic was replaced by Mr. Martic and so we're not going to continue in 1994 with your experiences during that time and beyond. Do you recall, was Norway the last time you ever met with Mr. Hadzic, or were there any subsequent?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: I do not know right now. Because after the Operation Storm, there was only Sector East left in Serb hands. And Stoltenberg and Kai Eide, we travelled to Belgrade and to Zagreb, and when Misa Milosevic told me that there should be now negotiations on the peaceful solution for Sector East and that these should not be led by the politicians from Knin but by politicians from the area and Mr. Hadzic would be one of them. The negotiations were actually then led by Stoltenberg and the American Ambassador in Zagreb, Peter Galbraith, and I think in the beginning Hadzic was there. I don't -- I'm not fully sure. I was also there but I did not sit in, and at least he was not one of the people who signed this -- this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event now this --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: That was Erdut 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is Erdut 2. This would have been in late 1995?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS
utterances.text: Yeah. Holbrooke wanted this to parallel the Dayton Peace Accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, thank you for your attention and your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. We'll start cross-examination tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Gosnell, you agree to that, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, this is the end of the today's hearing. We expect you back in court tomorrow at 9.00 for cross-examination by the Defence. This means that you are still under oath, and that, as a consequence, you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody, and you cannot talk to any of the parties. If that is clear, we thank you very much for today, and the court usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of August, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.55 p.m.,
